outcomes: Names what an opponent's last move threatens: a capture, a mate, or an attack on two pieces at once
Answers a real threat in a fitting way: moving, capturing, blocking or guarding
Tells a real threat from an attack that fails (guarded target with a bad recapture count, pinned attacker)
Says when the last move threatens nothing, and asks the same question about their own move

steps.prompt: Before anything is explained: why do you think Black pushed that pawn, and what would you do as White? Write one line. There is no wrong answer yet.

steps.caption: Watch what happens if White does not notice the pawn.

line.say: White makes an unrelated move and ignores the pawn.
The pawn takes the knight, and no white piece can take back.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
If White passes, Black comes out at least two points ahead.

steps.caption: The same position, but now White does notice and answers the threat.

line.say: The knight steps to a square the pawn does not attack.
Black has nothing to take, so the threat has gone.

claims.statement: No black piece attacks the knight on b3.

steps.text: A **threat** is the strongest thing your opponent could start with their *next* move if you did nothing: win something loose, give checkmate, or attack two pieces at once. It can be a short forcing line, not only one capture. Ask it after **every** opponent move, before your own plan. Why: your plan was made for the position before their move, and their move is the only new fact, so look there first. [H] I think skipping this look causes many club blunders; I have not measured it.

steps.caption: Black to move. Watch the rook's last move, and what it makes possible.

line.say: The rook moves to the c-file. Look at where it now points.
White plays an unrelated move and does not look.
The rook slides down the file and takes the bishop. Nothing takes back.

claims.statement: After the rook move the bishop on c3 is attacked and undefended.
No white piece defends the bishop on c3.

steps.caption: Same position, White to move. This time White checks what Black's last move attacked.

line.say: The bishop leaves the c-file for a square nothing attacks.
The rook has nothing left to take.

claims.statement: After the bishop moves no white piece is attacked and undefended.

steps.text: After each opponent move, look at four things. **Where did the moved piece go, and what does it attack now?** **What line did it open?** A piece that steps aside can unmask one behind it. **Is any piece of mine loose?** Attacked and undefended: check it first. **Does it give check or pin something?** A pinned piece cannot move freely. With two threats at once, look for one move that answers both, such as capturing the attacker.

steps.caption: Black to move. A bishop is about to step aside, and the rook behind it is the real danger.

line.say: The bishop steps off the e-file. It attacks nothing important, but it uncovers the rook.
White plays on without checking what the last move opened.
The rook runs down the open file and takes the undefended knight.

claims.statement: After the bishop moves the knight on e2 is attacked and undefended.
While the bishop stands on e6 nothing attacks the knight.

steps.caption: Same position, White to move. White sees the uncovered rook and answers it.

line.say: The knight leaves the e-file and goes where the rook cannot reach it.
Black has nothing to take.

claims.statement: Before the knight moves, it is attacked and undefended.
After the knight moves nothing is attacked and undefended.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's bishop pins the knight to the king, and a pawn also attacks it. A pinned piece cannot step away.

line.say: White makes an unrelated move.
The pawn takes the pinned knight, which could not leave.

claims.statement: The pinned knight has no legal move.
A black pawn attacks the knight.
If White passes, Black comes out ahead.

steps.text: Three kinds of threat come up again and again. You have met the first: **winning a piece** that is loose. The second is **checkmate**. The third is **attacking two things with one move**, such as your king and a piece, so that you can only save one. People call that last one a **fork**.

steps.caption: Black to move. White has just put a rook on the open e-file. Is it a threat?

line.say: Black ignores the rook and plays an unrelated move.
The rook lands on e8 with check. The pawns shut the king in and nothing covers e8: checkmate.

claims.statement: White threatens Re8 checkmate.
No black piece covers e8.

steps.caption: Black spotted the threat and played a pawn move. Does the same rook move still mate?

line.say: The rook still gives check on e8.
But the king walks to h7, the square the pawn move gave it. No mate.

claims.statement: Re8 is check but not checkmate.
The square h7 is empty, so the king can go there.

steps.text: A piece standing **behind** another on the same line backs it up. A queen with a bishop behind it on a diagonal is guarded through the queen: if the queen captures, the bishop covers that square. That can turn a capture the king could answer into one it cannot. [I] This idea sits behind many mating threats against a castled king.

steps.caption: White to move. The queen and bishop line up towards h2. Is that a threat?

line.say: White plays an unrelated move.
The queen takes h2 with check. The bishop behind it guards the square, and the rook blocks the king's last exit: checkmate.

claims.statement: If White passes, Qxh2 is checkmate.
Only the king guards h2.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's knight has just jumped to d4. Nothing of White's is attacked yet.

line.say: White sees nothing attacked and plays an unrelated move.
The knight jumps to e2 with check. From there it also attacks the rook.
White must answer the check first, so the rook cannot be saved.
The knight takes the rook.

claims.statement: No white piece is attacked right now.
No white piece covers e2.
From e2 the knight attacks both the king on g1 and the rook on c1.
If White passes, the knight wins the rook.

steps.caption: Black to move. White spotted the jump and put the rook where it covers e2.

line.say: Black tries the fork anyway.
The rook covers e2 and simply takes the knight.

claims.statement: The rook on e1 covers e2.
Ne2 just loses the knight.

steps.text: Eugene Znosko-Borovsky, in *The Middle Game in Chess* (1922), split threats into direct ones, which act at once, and distant ones, which show only over several moves, and said the decisive role belongs to the distant ones. [I] My reading: a fork is a direct threat, so the distant kind is what later lessons train.

steps.caption: White to move. One pawn move has attacked two knights at once.

line.say: White plays an unrelated move.
The pawn takes one knight.
White saves the other knight, but a piece is gone.

claims.statement: A black pawn attacks the knight on c4.
The same pawn attacks the knight on e4.
If White passes, Black wins a knight.

steps.text: Once a threat is real, you have four basic answers. **Move** the target away. **Capture** the attacker. **Block** the line it uses; that works only against a bishop, rook or queen, never a knight or a pawn. **Guard** the target so taking it costs something. A fifth, **counter-threat**, works only if their capture would be met by mate or a bigger capture of yours, so count first. [H] Beginners may reach for 'move away' by habit; I have not measured it.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop attacks a loose rook. The attacker itself can be captured.

line.say: The pawn takes the bishop that carried the threat. The threat disappears with it.
Black has lost a whole piece and nothing is threatened any more.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 is attacked and nothing guards it.
If White ignores the bishop, it wins the rook.
The pawn on h3 attacks the bishop.
Capturing the bishop wins at least a piece.

steps.caption: White to move. A rook attacks the loose bishop along the d-file. Put something in the way.

line.say: The knight steps between the rook and the bishop, and the e-pawn guards it.
If the rook took the knight, the pawn would take the rook, so Black looks for something else.

claims.statement: The bishop on d3 is attacked and nothing guards it.
If White ignores the rook, it wins the bishop.
After the block, no black piece attacks the bishop.
The blocking knight is guarded once.
After the block, no white piece is loose.

steps.caption: White to move. One knight attacks both the bishop and the knight. Look for one move that answers both.

line.say: Capturing the attacker removes both threats at once, and wins the knight.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 is attacked and nothing guards it.
Taking the knight wins a piece.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop attacks the loose knight. This time guard it.

line.say: A pawn now guards the knight.
If the bishop takes, the pawn takes back. The swap is even, so nothing is lost.
The pawn recaptures and White has lost nothing.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing guards it.
If White ignores the bishop, it wins the knight.
After the pawn move, no white piece is loose.
The knight is now guarded once.

steps.caption: The fifth answer. White to move. The bishop attacks the loose knight, but White has a bigger idea.

line.say: The rook makes a threat of its own: the back rank is open, and the rook now aims at d8.
Black needs to deal with the mate threat on d8, for example by making room for the king. The counter-threat bought only one move.
The knight still had to be saved, and now it is safe.

claims.statement: The knight on c4 is attacked and nothing guards it.
After the rook move, the rook attacks d8.

steps.caption: What if Black grabs the knight instead? White to move.

line.say: The back rank is open and nothing covers d8: checkmate. The bigger threat won.

claims.statement: The rook on d8 is checkmate.

steps.caption: An answer that fails. White blocks with the knight, but nothing guards it.

line.say: The knight steps between the rook and the bishop.
The rook simply takes the blocker. The block was loose, so it only moved the loss.

claims.statement: After the block, the knight on d4 is attacked and unguarded.
The block is a clear mistake.

steps.text: After you pick a reply, ask the question again about the reply itself. A block can leave the blocker loose, and a retreat can land on an attacked square. [I] A habit worth trying: before you let go of the piece, say aloud what your move leaves loose.

Not every attack is a real threat. Before you worry, ask three questions. **What would they take?** **After my recapture, who is ahead?** Count points: pawn 1, knight or bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9 (a rough convention). **Can they really play it?** A covered square, or an escape square for my king, can cancel a threat. If they gain no material and no mate, there is no immediate threat. [I] Positional threats exist but are outside this lesson.

steps.caption: White to move. The rook attacks the bishop, but a pawn defends it.

line.say: White ignores the attack.
The rook takes the bishop.
The pawn takes the rook. Black gave 5 points for 3.

claims.statement: The rook attacks the bishop.
The pawn on b3 defends the bishop.
Rxc4 bxc4 loses material for Black.

steps.caption: Since nothing is threatened, White can use the move for its own plan.

line.say: [I] One plan: bring the king nearer the middle if the game is heading for an ending.
Black still has no way to win anything.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose.

steps.text: Znosko-Borovsky (*The Middle Game in Chess*, 1922) called a threat fictitious when carrying it out would gain nothing, yet he held that it still ties the opponent down and turns real if they forget it [V-sheet]. [I] Limit of this lesson: it covers threats that act within one move. Deeper ones come later.

steps.caption: White to move. Now a pawn does the attacking. The knight is defended, yet this threat is real.

line.say: White ignores the pawn.
The pawn takes the knight.
White takes the pawn back. White gave 3 points and won only 1.

claims.statement: A black pawn attacks the knight.
The pawn on b3 defends the knight.
If White passes, Black comes out two points ahead.

steps.caption: Same position. White spots the pawn and moves the knight away from it.

line.say: The knight steps to e5, a square no black pawn attacks right now.
Black has no capture, so the threat is over.

claims.statement: No black pawn attacks e5 after the knight arrives.

steps.text: Here is a **rule of thumb**, not a law. An attack by a cheaper piece on a more valuable one needs an answer, even if the target is defended. A pawn attacking a knight is a threat. A rook attacking a bishop that a pawn defends usually is not. Check the recapture, count the points, then decide.

A swap on one square is a count. Say two black pieces attack a pawn that two white pieces guard. Each side stops as soon as the next capture would lose material. [I] A rule of thumb, not a law: capture with the cheapest piece first, and count before the first capture.

steps.caption: Black to move. Two black pieces attack e5 and two white pieces guard it. Count before capturing.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn.
The pawn takes the knight.
The rook takes the pawn.
The rook takes the rook. Black has lost a knight and a rook for two pawns.

claims.statement: Two black pieces attack e5.
Two white pieces guard e5.
Starting the exchange loses material for Black.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's rook sits on the open e-file. Does it threaten checkmate?

line.say: Black ignores the rook, because the bishop on d7 already covers e8.
The rook gives check on e8.
The bishop takes the rook. White gave a whole rook for nothing.

claims.statement: The bishop on d7 covers e8.
Re8 loses the rook for nothing.

steps.text: Now one position, changed one piece at a time. Predict first: in each version, is the bishop's attack a real threat, and why? Then step through the boards, which also show a pin.

steps.title: One change at a time
steps.prompt: The black bishop stands on b6 in all three. First nothing guards the knight. Second, a pawn guards it. Third, only a far-away white pawn has moved. Predict each verdict, then check.

steps.caption: The original. White to move. Black's bishop looks at the knight.

line.say: White makes an unrelated move.
The bishop takes the knight and nothing takes back.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing guards it.
If White passes, the bishop wins the knight.

steps.caption: Change one: a white pawn now stands on e3. Is the knight still in danger?

line.say: White makes an unrelated move.
The bishop takes the knight.
The pawn takes the bishop. A knight for a bishop is an even swap.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose now.
One white pawn guards the knight.
If White passes, the capture gains Black nothing.

steps.caption: Change two: instead of a pawn, a white rook stands on b1. The bishop's king is behind it.

line.say: White makes an unrelated move.
Black cannot play the capture: the bishop is pinned to its king and may not leave the b-file.

claims.statement: The bishop has no legal move at all.
The bishop does attack the knight, but only on paper.

steps.text: Two common ways a real-looking threat fails, and you can check both in seconds. The target is **guarded**: count the points after the recapture, and if the capture gains nothing or loses material, there is no threat. Or the attacker is **pinned**: the capture would be illegal. [I] These are not the only ways; an in-between check can also change the count. Ask before you spend a move on a defence.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's bishop on e6 looks towards the a2 pawn. Is that a threat?

line.say: White makes a quiet move of its own.
The bishop takes the pawn.
A defender takes the bishop. Black gave 3 points for 1.

claims.statement: The bishop attacks the a2 pawn.
The rook on a1 and the knight on c3 both defend it.
No white piece is loose.
Bxa2 Rxa2 loses material for Black.

steps.caption: Because nothing is threatened, White uses the move to improve a piece.

line.say: The rook comes to the open d-file, where it has more room.
Black takes the same file, and play goes on.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose.

steps.text: You make threats too, and every threat costs your opponent a move. The best ones are quiet: they improve your position *and* ask a question your opponent must answer. [H] At our level people often make a threat by accident, then forget to follow it up. Saying 'my move threatens...' aloud may fix that. I have not tested this.
steps.chapter: Make it, stop it, see it

steps.caption: White to move. Nothing is attacked on either side. Make a threat with a developing move.

line.say: The rook takes the open file and now attacks the loose pawn on d5.
Black spends a move on its king, so the threat has already cost Black time.

claims.statement: At the start, Black threatens nothing.
After the rook move the pawn on d5 is attacked and unguarded.

steps.caption: The position after the rook move. Black to move. What if Black ignores it?

line.say: Black plays an unrelated move.
The rook takes the pawn that nothing guarded.

claims.statement: If Black passes, the rook wins the pawn.
No black piece guards d5.

steps.text: The same question protects you from your own moves: *what would they threaten after I play this?* Dan Heisman, as reported in a chess.com article [S], uses 'hope chess' for moving and hoping the reply is harmless, and suggests looking at forcing replies first. A move can leave a piece loose that it used to guard.

steps.caption: White to move. The rook attacks the bishop, and the knight is its only guard. A developing move tempts.

line.say: The knight develops, and that takes away the bishop's only guard.
The rook takes the bishop and nothing takes back.

claims.statement: Now no white piece is loose: the knight guards the bishop.
After the knight leaves, the bishop is loose.
The developing move is a clear mistake.

steps.caption: Same position. Ask the question first, then pick a move that keeps the knight where it is. Kf1, b3 and a3 all do.

line.say: The king steps towards the centre, and the knight keeps guarding the bishop.
Black has found nothing to take.

claims.statement: After the king move, no white piece is loose.
After b3 no white piece is loose either.
The knight still guards the bishop.

steps.text: Now mixed positions with no labels. Some hold a real threat; in others nothing is threatened, and 'nothing' is a correct answer. Emanuel Lasker (*Common Sense in Chess*, Lectures 1 and 6) criticises rook-pawn moves played out of fear of a threat that does not yet exist. [V-sheet] [I] My reading: asking is cheap, but inventing a danger costs you a move.

steps.title: Same rook, one change
steps.prompt: Black's rook is on the open file. Black has just moved, and one piece differs each time. In which versions is there a real threat?

steps.text: A famous old trap is usually credited to a game of Légal against Saint Brie, Paris, 1787 [R: from memory, no source checked here]. The trap itself is taught in the opening-traps lessons; here it is only practice for the question. White has just made a surprising move. What does it threaten?

steps.caption: Black to move. Black sees a free queen and takes it. The bishop was giving a mating threat, and taking the knight on e5 would have removed it.

line.say: Black takes the queen, the biggest prize on the board.
White does not recapture. The bishop takes f7 with check.
The king has only one square.
The knight gives checkmate. All the king's squares are covered.

claims.statement: If Black takes the queen with Bxd1, then Bxf7+ Ke7 Nd5 is checkmate.
Taking the queen is legal.

steps.caption: The same position. Black asks what the last move threatened and takes the knight instead.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight, so the bishop's check on f7 no longer comes with a mating net.
White takes the bishop that had been attacked, and is still about two pawns ahead (Stockfish 19 lite, depth 18 [V]).

claims.statement: Taking the knight is Black's best move (engine, depth 16 [V]).
White is still about two pawns ahead after best play (Stockfish 19 lite, depth 18 [V]).

steps.prompt: Black took the queen at once. Name the first question Black skipped, and describe one moment in your own games where you are most likely to skip it.

fields.label: Where I am most likely to skip it

steps.text: [H] A guess, not a tested fact: many lost pieces at your level come from one-move threats you could have seen by asking the question once. I have no data on this. Test it on your own games: find a loss, and look for the first opponent move whose threat you did not answer.

**What to remember.** A threat is what they could do next if I passed. Look at where the moved piece went, what line it opened, and which of my pieces are loose. Answer a real one by moving, capturing, blocking or guarding. Check it is real: guarded target and recapture count, pinned attacker. Then ask the same question of my own move before I play it.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine a beginner who has just lost a piece to a move they did not see coming. Write what you would tell them. Then check yourself: did you say when the question helps, when a threat is not real, give an example they could set up on a board, and name one mistake to avoid?

fields.label: What to look at, and when a threat is not real
An example a beginner could set up on a board
